exs.name: TRX chest stretch
exs.tip: Stand beside the anchor, one arm extended back holding a handle, and rotate your torso away until you feel a stretch across the chest and front shoulder. Hold 30 seconds. Switch sides. Do this before any pressing — it improves shoulder range and reduces injury risk on push days.

exs.name: Arm circles + shoulder rolls
exs.tip: Stand tall, arms at sides. Circle both arms forward 10 times — start small and gradually widen the arc. Reverse for 10. Then shrug both shoulders up toward ears and roll them back and down in slow circles. This warms up the full rotator cuff and primes the shoulder joint for overhead and pressing work.

exs.name: Scapular retractions
exs.tip: Stand or sit tall. Squeeze your shoulder blades together as hard as you can — think about trying to hold a pencil between them. Hold for 2 seconds, then fully release. This activates the mid-back muscles that stabilise every pushing and pulling movement. Critical for shoulder health.

exs.name: World's greatest stretch
exs.muscles: Hip flexors · thoracic spine · glutes · hamstrings
exs.tip: Step into a deep lunge. Place the same-side hand on the floor beside your foot, then rotate your opposite arm up toward the ceiling, following it with your eyes. Hold briefly, return, and repeat. This single movement opens the hips, thoracic spine, and shoulders simultaneously — one of the highest-value warm-up drills available.

exs.name: Push-up (+ progressions)
exs.tip: Hands shoulder-width apart, body a straight line from head to heels — no hips sagging or piking. Lower your chest to just above the floor with elbows at roughly 45° from your body, then press back up. Progression order: standard → decline (feet on chair or step) → archer (one arm extended wide while the other presses) → one-arm. Move to the next level when you can complete all 4 sets cleanly.

exs.name: Pike push-up
exs.tip: Start in a downward-dog position with your hips high, forming a triangle with the floor. Bend your elbows and lower your forehead toward the floor between your hands, then press back up. The steeper the angle of your body, the more this becomes a shoulder-dominant movement and the less it resembles a chest press. Elevating your feet makes it harder and shifts load further onto the shoulders.

exs.name: TRX Y-fly
exs.muscles: Anterior deltoid · upper traps · serratus anterior
exs.tip: Face the TRX anchor with feet forward, lean back to create tension — the further back you lean, the harder it gets. With arms straight and thumbs pointing up, raise both arms up and out to form a Y overhead. Control the lowering phase completely. This replaces the band overhead press. Unlike a strict press, it keeps continuous tension throughout the range of motion, which the band couldn't do at higher loads.

exs.name: Dumbbell lateral raise
exs.tip: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing your thighs, slight soft bend at the elbows. Raise both arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height — no higher. At the top, your pinkies should be slightly higher than your thumbs, as if pouring water from a jug. Control the lowering over 2–3 seconds — the eccentric is where most of the growth stimulus comes from. Start very light: handle-only or 1.25kg per side. Replaces TRX T-raise with a more direct lateral deltoid stimulus.

exs.name: TRX tricep extension
exs.tip: Face away from the anchor. Hold the handles with elbows bent to 90°, hands near your forehead, and lean your body forward — the more forward you lean, the harder it is. Extend both elbows by pressing your forearms forward and up, keeping your upper arms fixed and elbows high throughout. Lower slowly with control. The instability of the TRX forces your core to work as a stabiliser at the same time.

exs.name: Plank hold
exs.tip: Forearms on the mat, elbows directly under your shoulders, body a straight line from head to heels. Squeeze your glutes hard and brace your core as if you're about to take a punch. Breathe steadily and don't hold your breath. When your form breaks — hips dropping or piking, lower back arching — stop. Quality beats duration every time. Build from 30 seconds toward 60 before adding time.

exs.name: Dead bug
exs.muscles: Deep core · hip flexors · lower back stabilisers
exs.tip: Lie on your back, arms pointing straight to the ceiling, knees bent at 90° directly above your hips. The critical cue: press your entire lower back into the mat and keep it there throughout every rep. Slowly lower your right arm overhead and left leg toward the floor simultaneously, stopping just before your back lifts, then return and switch sides. This works the deep core in a way that sit-ups don't, with no sliding.

exs.name: Side plank
exs.tip: Elbow directly under your shoulder, feet stacked or staggered for stability. Lift your hips so your body forms a straight diagonal line from head to heels — resist the urge to let your top hip roll forward. Keep your gaze forward, not down. Progress by adding hip dips (the Session B version) once 30 seconds feels manageable.

exs.name: VOR tracking (chiropractor)
exs.tip: Semi-tandem stance: take a half step forward with feet on either side of an imaginary midline. Extend one arm with thumb up, cover the other eye with your free hand. Tracking your thumb with your open eye, sweep your arm slowly all the way up over your head and back down (vertical plane), then repeat sweeping side to side (horizontal). Switch which foot is forward and repeat. This trains your vestibulo-ocular reflex — the integration of balance, vision, and movement that supports everything from running to skating.

exs.name: Single leg balance
exs.tip: Stand on one foot with a soft knee bend, gaze fixed on a still point in front of you. Hold 30 seconds. Then close your eyes — this removes visual input and forces your vestibular and proprioceptive systems to work harder. It's dramatically more difficult. Progress over weeks by adding slow head turns while balancing, then arm movements.

exs.name: TRX chest stretch
exs.tip: Stand beside the anchor holding a single handle, arm extended behind you. Rotate your torso away from the anchor until you feel the stretch across your chest and front shoulder. Hold 30 seconds and switch. Especially useful before a pull session because tight chest muscles restrict how far you can retract your shoulder blades during rows.

exs.name: Band pull-aparts
exs.tip: Hold the band at shoulder width with both hands in front of you, arms straight. Pull the band apart by driving both hands outward until you reach a T-shape, squeezing your rear delts hard at the end range. Use your lightest band — this is activation work, not loading work. Keep the bands for low-tension exercises only.
exs.warn: Light bands only — use lowest tension available

exs.name: Cat-cow + scapular retractions
exs.tip: On hands and knees: arch your back up (cat) then dip it down and lift your head (cow). Move slowly through 10 full cycles. Then transition to seated or standing scapular retractions — squeeze shoulder blades together as far as possible, hold 2 seconds, release fully. This primes the mid-back muscles that drive every pulling movement in this session.

exs.name: Single-arm dumbbell row
exs.muscles: Lats · rhomboids · rear deltoid · biceps · core
exs.tip: Place one knee and the same-side hand on the couch for support, body roughly parallel to the floor. Let the dumbbell hang with a straight arm, shoulder fully relaxed. Initiate by retracting your shoulder blade, then drive your elbow straight back and up — keep it close to your body. Squeeze hard at the top, then lower with a fully straight arm. This is your primary progressive overload exercise: log the weight every session and add 1.25kg when you complete all 4 sets cleanly.
exs.note: Priority exercise — replaces TRX row. Track weight each session and increase load systematically. Primary driver for your arm deficit.

exs.name: TRX face pull
exs.muscles: Rear deltoid · external rotators · rhomboids · lower traps
exs.tip: Face the anchor with arms extended at eye level. Pull both hands toward your face with your elbows flaring high and wide — elbows at or above shoulder height, not pulling back and down like a row. End position: thumbs plugging your ears, elbows wide, palms facing forward. The external rotation at the top is the whole point — it trains the rotator cuff in a way rows can't. Hold for one second at peak contraction. Alternative if no TRX available: band pull-aparts — hold a band at shoulder width, pull to a T-shape, squeeze rear delts at end range.

exs.name: Hammer curl
exs.tip: Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing each other — thumbs pointing up throughout, never rotating. Keeping elbows pinned to your sides, curl both dumbbells toward your shoulders. The neutral grip shifts emphasis onto the brachialis, which sits underneath the bicep and adds significant thickness to the upper arm when developed. Lower slowly over 3 seconds.

exs.name: Dumbbell bicep curl
exs.tip: Hold a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing forward. Keeping your elbows pinned to your sides, curl both dumbbells toward your shoulders. As you curl, actively supinate your wrists — rotate so pinkies turn up — to maximise bicep activation. Squeeze hard at the top. Lower slowly over 3 seconds: the eccentric produces more growth stimulus than the curl itself. Track weight and progress like the row.

exs.name: TRX plank (feet in straps)
exs.tip: Place both feet in the TRX foot cradles with toes pointed. Walk your hands out until you're in a push-up position with straight arms. Brace everything — squeeze your glutes, brace your core, push the floor away with your hands. The instability of the suspension trainer means your core has to work significantly harder than on a floor plank. Start with 20 seconds and build from there.

exs.name: Plank shoulder taps
exs.tip: High plank position on straight arms. Keeping your hips absolutely level — this is everything — lift your right hand and tap your left shoulder, then return it to the floor before moving the other hand. If your hips rock side to side, widen your foot stance slightly until you can control it, then narrow over time. Slow and controlled is the only way this exercise does what it's supposed to do.

exs.name: Hollow hold
exs.muscles: Transverse abdominis · rectus abdominis · hip flexors
exs.tip: Lie on your back and press your entire lower back into the floor — this is the non-negotiable starting point. Extend arms overhead and legs straight, then lift arms, head, shoulders and legs slightly off the floor. The lower your legs, the harder it is. If your lower back lifts off the floor at any point, raise your legs higher until it doesn't. This is a gymnastics staple and one of the best pure anterior core exercises.

exs.name: Side plank with hip dip
exs.tip: Get into a side plank — elbow under shoulder, body straight. From there, lower your hip toward the floor without touching it, then drive it back up past neutral, pausing briefly at the top. One dip + one drive = one rep. Keep your torso from rotating throughout — the rotation is the failure mode. This is the loaded progression from the static side plank in Session A.

exs.name: Single leg RDL (bodyweight)
exs.tip: Stand on one leg with a soft knee bend. Hinge at your hip — not your waist — and reach your torso forward while your free leg extends straight behind you as a counterbalance. Think of your body as a lever pivoting at the hip, not folding at the spine. Hold the lowest position for one second, then drive through your glute to return to standing. Your legs are already strong from hockey — the challenge here is balance and control, not strength.

exs.name: VOR tracking (chiropractor)
exs.tip: Semi-tandem stance, one eye covered, track your thumb through the vertical and horizontal planes. Switch foot position and repeat. The progression over the coming weeks is to narrow your stance: semi-tandem → near-tandem → full heel-to-toe tandem. The heel-to-toe position removes almost all base of support and forces near-total reliance on your vestibular system. Expect this to take months to master.

exs.name: Single leg balance
exs.tip: Hold for 30 seconds on each leg with eyes open, then repeat with eyes closed. In Session B, after the single leg RDL, your stabilisers will be more fatigued — so the balance challenge is harder than it looks. Progress by adding slow head turns left and right while holding the balance.
